newsitem.title: USA: Jobless shocks worse in welfare states - Chicago Fed.
newsitem.headline: Jobless shocks worse in welfare states - Chicago Fed.

text.p: Economies that offer generous safety nets to the unemployed are far less likely to absorb shocks than countries providing limited benefits, according to a Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago paper.
"In turbulent economic times, the welfare state is less conducive to handling that situation. You lose a lot of human capital," Chicago Fed economist Lars Ljungqvist told Reuters on Tuesday.
"In a more 'laissez-faire' economy, like the United States, where everyone would have to fend for himself, these economic distortions would not come into play," he added.
Ljungqvist co-authored the paper "The European Unemployment Dilemma" with academic Thomas Sargent.

While most research ties Europe's high unemployment rate to the demand side of labor -- such as hiring and firing costs -- Ljungqvist and Sargent focus on the supply side of labor, or the "search intensity" among laid-off workers and the increasing loss of their skills over time.
"The incentives are not there for workers to find a new job in a welfare state," the Chicago Fed economist noted.
Yet Ljungqvist asserted that jobless benefits by themselves cannot be blamed for high and extended unemployment.

The Chicago Fed economist noted unemployment remained low in Europe in the 1960s and 1970s despite generous benefits. However, unemployment worsened markedly in Europe's welfare states after the 1970s and has not recovered since.
"More than half of all European unemployment in 1989 was classified as long-term unemployment with a duration of a year and over, up from less than a third of unemployment in 1979," Ljungqvist said.
At the same time, laissez-faire countries such as the United States experienced wide fluctuations in unemployment that were quickly corrected, Ljungqvist said.
The Chicago Fed's study shows the U.S. unemployment rate averaging 6.7 percent in 1974-79 and 7.2 percent in 1980-89. It has trended lower since.
In Europe, that rate averaged 4.7 percent in 1974-79 and 9.2 percent in 1980-1989 and has remained on an upward trend.

"The transient (economic) shock results in a prolonged period of long-term unemployment in the welfare state whereas the recovery is almost immediate in the laissez-faire economy," Ljungqvist said. "The welfare economy has considerably more dispersion in the duration of unemployment spells."
The Ljungqvist-Sargent model shows the unemployment rate in both "welfare" and "laissez-faire" economies spiking up due to a shock to the economy -- but followed by two very different scenarios.
"In the laissez-faire economy, the high unemployment rate dies out pretty quickly when the unemployed workers bite the bullet," Ljungqvist said.

"In contrast, the welfare economy is plagued by a prolonged period of unemployment since the unemployed workers with their depreciated skills have difficulty finding jobs that (match) their compensation," he added.
Among the shocks affecting European countries for nearly two decades, Ljungqvist cited the impact of broad technology changes and economic globalization on industrialized nations.
"It's more than two decades of ongoing economic turbulence from many different sources--technology, restructuring, globalization," the Chicago Fed economist said.
Ljungqvist declined to say whether the limited U.S. unemployment safety net is a factor accounting for the low current jobless rate in America.

"It is important to keep in mind this study is not really suited for short-term variations in the unemployment rate. There still is some debate among economists about the natural rate of unemployment," Ljungqvist also said.
The Chicago Fed economist concluded "the welfare state of today would benefit from restructuring. It is more important than ever to incorporate incentives to work.
"Failure to do so threatens to produce high and long-term unemployment and needlessly to waste human capital," he said.
